title: Runtime plugin integration experiments: Triton + TensorRT plugin strategy
content:
Summary:
This note captures a set of focused experiments and implementation notes for integrating TensorRT (TRT) custom plugins with Triton in our serving runtime. The emphasis is on memory behavior, scheduler interactions, and KV cache semantics when mixing native TRT engines, Triton backends, and our custom CUDA kernels. The goal is to produce a recommended runtime pattern that minimizes tail latency regressions while retaining cost-efficient throughput.

Motivation and scope:
- We have multiple models where TRT engines give significant per-token cost savings, but we see intermittent latency spikes and memory fragmentation under long-lived processes.
- Triton simplifies model lifecycle and multi-model serving, but Triton+TRT plugin combinations introduce lifetime and allocator interactions that are under-specified for our workloads.
- This doc focuses on: plugin loading/unloading, GPU allocator strategy (cudaMalloc/free vs pooled allocators), KV cache placement (GPU resident vs CPU pinned vs hybrid), scheduler interactions (batching, preemption, inter-model fairness), and safe fallbacks.

Goals:
1) Define plugin lifecycle best practices to avoid fragmentation and memory leaks across hot reloads and model rollouts.
2) Propose scheduler heuristics that balance batch throughput and tail latency across mixed TRT/Triton/custom kernels.
3) Recommend KV cache placement and eviction policies for sharded multi-tenant workloads.
4) Produce an experiment matrix and preliminary results to validate hypotheses.

Background/observations so far:
- TRT engines that use IAllocator-based plugins (custom kernels) rely on Triton or model process allocators; differences in allocator lifetime cause orphaned GPU memory when Triton loads/unloads models frequently.
- Using cudaMalloc with repeated engine rebuilds increases fragmentation; pooled allocators (CUB/Jetson/tensorrt::IHostMemory reuse) reduce fragmentation but require deterministic deallocation ordering.
- KV cache on GPU dramatically reduces per-token latency for long sequences but consumes a lot of resident memory and complicates scheduling when multiple large contexts are active.
- CUDA graph warmup reduces kernel-launch overhead for stable shapes, but interacts poorly with dynamic batching.

Experiment matrix (design):
- Variables:
  * Backend mode: pure Triton ONNX -> Triton TRT backend -> TRT standalone in process
  * Allocator: cudaMalloc/free, polymorphic pooled allocator (per-model arena), thread-local per-stream pool
  * KV cache placement: GPU-resident per-model, GPU-sharded across models with LRU eviction, CPU-pinned with async prefetch to GPU, hybrid on-demand transfer of active shards
  * Scheduling: single global batching queue, per-model priority queues with weighted fair scheduling, preemptive slot for low-latency requests (SLO guard)
  * Fallback: automatic fallback to smaller-quantized engine, fallback to CPU-only path (rare), fallback to next-region instance
- Measurements:
  * P95/P99 latency, median latency, throughput (tokens/s), GPU memory high-water mark, fragmentation (measured by cudart free/total snapshots), eviction count, cold-start time for contended engines

Implementation notes and gotchas:
1) Plugin lifecycle and allocator ownership
   - Always ensure our TRT plugin implements IPluginV2DynamicExt::getWorkspaceSize and uses TRT IAllocator hooks where possible. If Triton manages the allocator, the model unload path must call plugin->terminate and free all plugin-held resources prior to engine destruction.
   - For Triton-managed processes, register a process-global pooled allocator that reports allocations using our tracing hooks. Provide a lightweight purge API that can be called during model unloads to defragment temporary pools.
   - Avoid mixing direct cudaMalloc and pooled allocations in the same allocation domain; pick one per plugin. Mixing causes fragmentation that cannot be reclaimed easily.

2) Memory fragmentation mitigation
   - Use per-stream CUDA arenas sized by per-model peak working set. Track high-water marks during SLO-compliance tests and provision arena sizes conservatively for dedicated pools.
   - Implement a periodic compaction task in the daemon that triggers between low-traffic windows: it serializes model reloads with a built-in GPU memory scrub (unload unused engines, release arenas, then reload on demand).

3) KV cache design patterns
   - Pattern A (GPU-resident per-model): best latency; simple but requires pinning large contiguous memory. Good for enterprise customers who purchase Dedicated capacity.
   - Pattern B (Sharded GPU with LRU): shard KV cache at chunk granularity (e.g., per-512-token slice). When memory pressure rises, evict least-recently-used shards and materialize them from CPU-resident stores on demand. Requires async prefetch to avoid blocking critical path.
   - Pattern C (CPU-pinned + on-demand transfer): store canonical KV on CPU pinned memory and transfer only active prefix to GPU. Lower memory footprint but higher per-token latency variance.
   - Eviction heuristics: prioritize eviction of older conversation shards, preferentially keep hot prefixes, and tie eviction to request-level timestamps and reuse frequency.

4) Scheduler heuristics and batching policies
   - For mixed workloads (short chat vs long completion), implement a two-tier scheduler:
     * Fast-path queue for short requests with strict latency budget (SLO guard) that bypasses large-batch aggregation if queue depth is small.
     * Bulk-path queue that aims for throughput by coalescing requests into larger continuous batches; use shape-aware batching to preserve CUDA graph applicability.
   - Preemption: lightweight cooperative preemption by interrupting batch formation when fast-path SLO is imminent. Avoid hard preemption inside kernels (not feasible) — instead prioritize request selection.
   - Weighted fair queuing: assign dynamic weights per model based on SLA tier, recent latency errors, and cost budget.

5) Fallback strategies
   - Multi-variant engines: keep a small quantized engine (e.g., int8) ready for cold start or degraded capacity. An in-memory mapping associates model -> [fp16_engine, int8_engine] with automatic fallback when memory or latency exceeds thresholds.
   - Safe CPU fallback: implement CPU reference path only for correctness checks and rarely for production; prefer region fallback or degraded engine before CPU to avoid catastrophic latency.

Observability and telemetry needed:
- Per-allocation telemetry: size, allocator type, timestamp, associated model and inference id.
- KV shard metrics: hits, misses, eviction counts, average residency time, load latency.
- Scheduler metrics: queue depths, batch sizes, time spent in queue, preemption events, per-route P50/P95/P99.
- Fragmentation metrics: periodic snapshots of total/free memory per device and fragmentation ratio (free / (total - reserved)).

Preliminary experiment results (short summary):
- Setup: 4x A100, mixed tenant workload simulating chat (short windowed requests) + long-form completion. Models: small chat model (2.5B), large completion (13B) converted to TRT and a smaller fp16 variant.
- Finding A: Switching pooled allocators (per-model arena) reduced median latency by ~6% and P99 by ~14% vs raw cudaMalloc under heavy churn (engine reloads every 30m).
- Finding B: GPU-resident KV cache improved median per-token latency for long completions by 35% vs CPU-pinned; however, with 6 concurrent large contexts memory pressure caused frequent LRU evictions leading to 3-4x increase in tail latency during eviction spikes.
- Finding C: Cooperative two-tier scheduler reduced short-request P95 by 22% while maintaining overall throughput within 7% of baseline.
- Finding D: Keeping a standby int8 engine reduced cold-period tail spikes when memory pressure forced eviction of bigger engines; switching cost averaged 120ms for our test harness.

Recommendations (engineering roadmap):
1) Adopt a per-model pooled allocator with explicit purge API. Integrate allocator telemetry into the console.
2) Implement KV cache sharding with async prefetch: use shard size tuned to typical prefix reuse (start with 512-token shards). Prefer GPU-resident shards for Dedicated customers and hybrid for hosted where multi-tenancy is heavier.
3) Build a two-tier scheduler prototype in the runtime that supports cooperative preemption and shape-aware batching. Explore a cost-model to pick weights for WFQ.
4) Implement fallback variant registry for models and an automatic fallback trigger based on memory high-water and latency SLO violations.
5) Define an operator-level lifecycle hook in Triton integration that guarantees plugin->terminate and allocator purge in model unload paths. Raise a runtime PR to add robust unload sequencing and test harness.

Next steps / experiments to run:
- Run extended churn test (72h) with model reload frequency at 5m/30m to surface fragmentation patterns across all allocator variants.
- Tune shard size and eviction threshold for KV sharded approach using production sampled traces.
- End-to-end SLO experiments with simulated tenant mixes to validate scheduler heuristics.
- Implement a small alpha of dynamic prefetch (predictive loading of likely next shards) for conversational flows.

Open questions / risks:
- How aggressive can we be with background compaction without impacting SLAs? Need better isolation window scheduling.
- Exact shard size tradeoff depends on model attention patterns; we need customer traces to tune.
- Triton internals may change allocator semantics across versions; maintain compatibility tests per Triton release and add graceful fallback when allocator hooks are missing.

Appendix: quick checklist for engineering tasks
- [ ] Add allocator purge hook in runtime unload path (PR: #832 referenced above).
- [ ] Implement per-model arena and expose config knobs in the runtime config + console.
- [ ] Build KV shard store (CPU pinned) and async prefetch pipeline.
- [ ] Add scheduler prototype, telemetry dashboards for queue/batch metrics.
- [ ] Run 72h churn test and gather fragmentation/latency traces for analysis.

Notes-to-self / loose ideas:
- Consider exploring NVLink-aware cross-GPU shard placement for Dedicated clusters to hold larger caches across devices.
- Investigate compacting device memory by migrating cold shards to a swap area device (if NVSwitch or NVLink available) before host eviction.

If you review this, please comment on the eviction heuristics and whether we should prioritize eviction by conversation age or conversation activity. Also call out any missing telemetry that would help debug fragmentation spikes.
